lines.narration: Sean goes where Han goes now. In a pachinko back room, Morimoto — DK's wingman — asks when the next race is. That is bait, not curiosity. Why not be in it, Han says, and the smile that cracks Sean's flat face is the first thing in Tokyo he has openly wanted.

claim.subject: the American in the white shirt

lines.narration: Terms land in nine seconds. Morimoto takes Han's 86 Corolla if Sean loses; Han puts up a 72 Skyline against it. Nobody once asks the kid whether he can drive.

claim.subject: the man in the black T-shirt

lines.narration: Then the table is finished with Sean — get him out of here. With him gone, they press Han about a shipment that has not arrived. Sit pretty and let me handle it, he says — easily, then his eyes drop and the smile is gone.

claim.subject: the long-haired man in the dark jacket

lines.narration: Out on the neon street Sean feeds a payphone and tells his father he had to stay late at school for extracurricular activities. The lie buys him the night.

claim.subject: the American in the white shirt

lines.narration: Neela has tracked him down. Stop following me around, he says; she only stopped by to ask his boyfriend for drifting lessons. He shuts it flat — she does not want to be part of this world.

claim.subject: the woman in the fur-collar coat

lines.narration: So she reads him back to himself. Army brat, moved around a lot, parents never home, so he walked around angry — and now he has swapped his family for a crowd of drift nuts. Zero for one, cowboy, he says, and neither of them buys it.
Driving home, Sean asks if everything is okay back there. Han says he can handle it. Then he lays out the actual shape of Tokyo.
DK's uncle Kamata takes a cut of everyone's action on his turf and keeps the police off them. Fifty percent of something beats a hundred percent of nothing, Han says, cheerful as weather.

Then they argue over what a race is for. Beating somebody only proves you are faster, Han says — it has to be for something that matters. So why let him race DK? DK's pride is his kryptonite — also, Sean still owes him a car.
The needle hits a hundred and ninety-seven and a patrol car slots in behind them. Sean's grin drops as he twists to look back.
Han does not even sit up. Police cars top out at a hundred and eighty, he says, so above that they will not even try. Sean floors it, and announces he is beginning to like this country already.

They pull in at Han's garage, which has a party bolted onto it. Han moves through it like a mayor, mobbed and kissed under the mirror ball. Sean trails two steps behind, known by nobody, left on the outside of all of it.

Twinkie, his one friend from school, hooks an arm round his neck and explains the economics of the room. These women have posed all day, know nobody in town, and every man here is too scared to approach them. So you talk to the little dude who makes you laugh.

Sean walks past a red Evo, and walks back to it. Han hands it over — not lends, hands. Sean represents him now, and Han will not let his name roll around Tokyo in a Hyundai. Generosity and branding in one breath.

The first thing Sean does with the gift is take it to a dockside lot and try to wreck it, slewing it through tyre smoke. On the sofas the crew laugh — a race coming against the best drifter in Tokyo, and he still cannot drift. He keeps going anyway.

Morning, school blazer. Boswell works a stripped coupe he found wrecked on the base — says it has potential. Then he offers a proverb he has clearly been saving: deru kui wa utarero. The nail that sticks out gets hammered. Good advice, and completely useless on this particular kid.

claim.subject: the grey-haired man in the grey henley

lines.narration: On the school roof Twinkie is pinned on the concrete while a blond classmate plays it up for a laughing crew. Sean shoves through the ring, hand raised, and calls it a misunderstanding. Standing quietly at the back of a crowd is the one thing he has never managed. The blond backs off, no punch thrown.

claim.subject: the young American in the school blazer

lines.narration: Twinkie rounds on him for wrecking business up here. Neela stays behind on the emptied deck. Not easy, saving the day, is it, she says — then tells him he is doing all right. First approval this city has handed him for free, and the thing between them still has a nickname and an uncle.
